So we keep talking about Ukrainian drones attacking Russian refineries. 

Pulling out my Refinery Configuration Schematic, I see 3 big scenarios:

1⃣If the drones struck the CDU (the crosses in blue), there's refinery downtime and the immediate hit is on distillates production and more crude exports.

2⃣If the drones struck the reformer (the small yellow crosses), you are going to get less mogas but more naphtha exports from Russia. 

3⃣If the drones struck the important secondary units like the FCC and HCU (the big red crosses), you are going to get less mogas and diesel respectively, and more fuel oil exports from Russia (if the CDU is still running). 

Also it usually takes a longer time to repair damaged secondary units vs the CDU due to more sophisticated parts.

I don't have visibility of where the strikes happened, but we can see European product cracks for direction.

quotedTweet.text:
Refinery 101 (and maybe a bit more)

Refining is complicated. Put in crude A in refinery B will give you different products than putting crude A in refinery C. 

Each unit in the refinery is unique and produces different products. Later you blend them back together to make a final product (like gasoline and fuel oil). What a strange system but that's how it works.

I have tried to simplify the main units to as simple terms as I can in the attached refinery configuration schematic. For those in the industry, you will say that's too simple. But those who are oil tourists, this is going to look like rocket science. 

Remember I talked about the min 60% requirement in the refinery? That limit applies to every single unit highlighted in the configuration schematic, not just the CDU. And there are countless more units that I have NOT shown in the chart (e.g. hydrotreaters, desalters, alkylation, etc).

Regardless, I do hope this helps explains some of the stuff that I have been talking about in the past few weeks. 

This week's @SpartaCommo podcast in particular talks about the way fuel oil gets upgraded and the hard choices the refinery has to make when you have less VGO and short residue available. 

Stay tuned. The stress is still in refined products and will be for some time.

#oott

Here's what I wrote in Oil Context Weekly today on this exact topic:

"Let’s begin with the 9 million barrels a day figure. According to our analysis using tanker tracking data from Kpler, the recent peak—over the past week or so—in confirmed Hormuz transits is roughly 7.5 MMbpd on a 7-day rolling basis (the same smoothing that Secretary Wright used). This is the highest level since the bust of the post-MOU breakout bump.

Let’s get one thing out of the way quickly: I have absolutely no doubt that the US government, and the US Navy specifically, has far better visibility of the ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz than we barrel counters—or the tanker tracking data providers on which we rely. That said, the Trump administration, including Wright, has a history of misleading or outright erroneous statements, which tend to lean in the direction of “everything is fine!” So, the immediate reaction to Wright’s 9 MMbpd Hormuz figure—as “obvious nonsense!”—was understandable.

While this figure is likely an overstatement, it’s not altogether implausible. In fact, we’ve been writing a lot, in these weekly updates, about the deterioration in the fidelity of super-recent tanker tracking data. This should reduce your confidence in any given tanker count, especially for very recent transits, given that many outbound tankers don’t get marked until they reappear on AIS after exiting the Strait entirely. Instead, I think the best description of Wright’s figure is plausible exaggeration rather than outright falsehood.

The error in Wright’s post is actually subtler, and relates to the claim of 5-7 MMbpd of Hormuz rerouting. These numbers are often conflated with the total exports from Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea or the UAE out of Fujairah; but, it’s important to remember that these were functioning export routes prior to the outbreak of the war. The actual incremental switching is, at best, 4 MMbpd between Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and you could maybe count a few hundred kbpd of Iraqi crude making its way to the Mediterranean via trucks through Syria if you were being generous.

Our estimate of total oil flows is closer to 12 MMbpd (i.e., 8 MMbpd Hormuz + 4 MMbpd reroutes) compared to Secretary Wright’s “approximately” 15 MMbpd of Middle Eastern oil outflow (i.e., 9 MMbpd Hormuz + 5-7 MMbpd reroutes). And we need to ensure we are using the correct baseline: that 12 MMbpd should then be benchmarked to the broader prewar Middle Eastern flow of ~23 MMbpd rather than the prewar ~20 MMbpd prewar Hormuz flow. Altogether, this implies that Middle Eastern oil exports are still only running at just more than 50% of prewar levels."

(and that's before we get to the issue that the reroute numbers depend on a fully functioning Saudi Red Sea trade which... let's just say isn't exactly a slam dunk atm)

U.S. residential electricity prices and political responses

In the United States, rapidly rising electricity prices have become a fiercely contested political issue at state and federal levels, fuelling broader concerns about the impact of large data centres on local communities and the cost of living. 

Average prices for residential customers are forecast to rise almost 6% in 2026 on top of an increase of 5% in 2025, according to estimates prepared by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).

The BCOM TR Index trades up 1.7% this month, taking its year-to-date gain to 25%, with advances seen across all sectors except energy, where WTI crude and natural gas are the only major contracts trading lower. Precious metals continue to lead, with a 7.4% monthly gain despite some end-of-week profit-taking, bringing the sector’s YTD performance back to flat. Agriculture follows with a 2.8% gain, led by sugar, cocoa and wheat, while industrial metals are up around 1% amid broad but relatively modest gains.
#CrudeOil has given back part of its geopolitical risk premium. Brent eased around 2% to near USD 87 after six consecutive gains, while WTI traded near USD 81 in early Friday dealing. The absence of fresh escalation around the still-closed Strait of Hormuz, combined with the previous week’s very large US inventory build, has encouraged some profit-taking. In our view, the pullback looks more like position-trimming than a fundamental change in the supply outlook, particularly while the Strait remains almost closed, and regional production and export capacity remain constrained.
Precious metals: #Gold trades lower for a second day as profit-taking sets in following a strong run of gains, with tame US inflation data and reduced expectations for further rate hikes largely priced in for now. Silver has slipped back below USD 64 after almost reaching USD 67 earlier in the week. Despite the pullback, the underlying backdrop remains supportive in our opinion, with lower rate expectations, renewed investor demand and continued official-sector buying helping underpin the sector.
Industrial metals: #Copper futures also traded lower on profit-taking following a week that delivered further supportive supply-side developments. Producers continue to struggle to maintain output levels, while robust demand and pre-tariff stockpiling in the US have drawn metal towards American warehouses, tightening the pool of readily available supply elsewhere. These dynamics continue to support an underlying tightening narrative despite the latest bout of price consolidation.
